title-group.article-title: Crebanine Protects HUVECs from LPS-Induced Inflammation and Oxidative Stress by Suppressing NF-κB Pathway

abstract.p: Endothelial dysfunction induced by inflammation and oxidative stress represents a critical pathological mechanism in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, including sepsis and atherosclerosis. Although crebanine has been reported to possess anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties, its effects on inflammation and oxidative stress in endothelial cells remain unknown. In this study, we assessed cell viability, apoptosis, and migration using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8), flow cytometry, and a wound healing assay, respectively. The levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the expression of inflammatory and oxidative stress markers were determined by qRT-PCR, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and Western blotting analysis. Our results demonstrated that crebanine alleviated lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced apoptosis and dysfunction in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Crebanine treatment inhibited the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), ROS, and malondialdehyde (MDA), while it enhanced the activity of the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase (SOD). Mechanistically, crebanine suppressed LPS-induced activation of the NF-κB signaling pathway in HUVECs. Furthermore, the improvement effect of crebanine on the inflammation and dysfunction in LPS-treated HUVECs was reversed by diprovocim, an NF-κB activator. These findings suggest that crebanine ameliorates LPS-induced inflammation and oxidative stress in HUVECs by inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway, indicating its potential therapeutic value for treating vascular endothelial dysfunction-related diseases.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Vascular endothelial cells play a key role in maintaining vascular homeostasis, including ensuring vascular integrity and permeability (Su et al., 2025). Endothelial cell dysfunction manifests as enhanced oxidative stress, sustained inflammatory response, and hyperpermeability, which exacerbates the progression of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases (Bloom et al., 2023; Immanuel and Yun, 2023). Endothelial dysfunction represents one of the earliest and most predominant pathological alterations in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, including sepsis and atherosclerosis (Mu et al., 2024). Therefore, there is an urgent need to investigate novel therapeutic approaches to ameliorate oxidative stress and inflammation in that induce endothelial cell dysfunction. Studies have shown that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces oxidative stress and inflammatory responses in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), a well-established model for studying vascular endothelial cell dysfunction (Guo et al., 2021).

In the last two decades, a large number of active compounds derived from natural products have been identified as potent chemotherapeutic agents. Crebanine is an aporphine alkaloid, which is widely found in natural plants such as Stephania venosa (Makarasen et al., 2011). It has attracted much attention due to its many proven biological activities and pharmacological safety. Previous studies have shown that crebanine exhibits therapeutic potential, including anti-inflammatory, anti-tumor, anti-arrhythmic, and neuroprotective effects (Yang et al., 2023; Yodkeeree et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021). However, to date, no studies have investigated the therapeutic effect of crebanine on LPS-stimulated HUVECs.

Extensive studies have confirmed that LPS can activate the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) signaling pathway in HUVECs to induce oxidative stress and inflammatory responses (Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025). Interestingly, it has been reported that crebanine reduces the proliferation, invasion and survival of TNF-α-stimulated A549 cells by inhibiting NF-κB activity and its downstream gene expression profile (Wang et al., 2021). Additionally, crebanine alleviates oxidative stress and neuroinflammation in microglia by suppressing the NF-κB signaling pathway (Yang et al., 2023). The aim of this study is to explore whether crebanine improves inflammatory responses and oxidative stress in LPS-treated HUVECs by regulating the NF-κB signaling pathway.

In this study, we found that crebanine enhanced the viability and tube-forming capacity of HUVECs exposed to LPS, while it reduced the levels of inflammatory factors and reactive oxygen species (ROS). Mechanistically, crebanine suppressed the LPS-induced activation of the NF-κB signaling pathway in HUVECs. In conclusion, our results demonstrate that crebanine alleviates LPS-induced inflammation, oxidative stress, and dysfunction in HUVECs by inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway, suggesting its potential for clinical therapeutic development.

sec.title: Chemicals and reagents
sec.p: Crebanine (Cat. #HY-N2255. purity 99.83%) and diprovocim (Cat. #HY-123942, purity 98.82%) were obtained from MedChemExpress (MCE, Monmouth Junction, NJ, USA). LPS (Cat. #ST1470) was obtained from Beyotime Biotechnology (Beyotime, Shanghai, China).

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: HUVECs were obtained from the Cyagen Biosciences Inc. (Cat. #HUVEC-20001, Jiangsu, China), and were cultured in OriCellTM Complete Medium (Cat. #HUVEC-90011, Cyagen Bioscience, Jiangsu, China) containing 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Cat. #A5873601, Gibco, Waltham, MA, USA) and 10% foetal bovine serum (Cat. #10091148, Gibco, Waltham, MA, USA) at 37°C with 5% CO2. The study was divided into four groups: DMSO, LPS (2 μg/mL), LPS+crebanine (20 μM), and LPS+crebanine (40 μM). In short, the cells were replaced with complete media containing crebanine for 24 h after LPS stimulation for 12 h, and then the supernatant and cells were collected for subsequent experiments. We used the classic NF-κB activator diprovocim to validate the underlying mechanism. The cells were cultured 12 h after LPS stimulation with complete media containing crebanine (40 μM) or crebanine (40 μM)+diprovocim (0.5 μM) for 24 h (Wu et al., 2024).

sec.title: Cell viability assay
sec.p: The Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay (Cat. #C0038, Beyotime, Shanghai, China) was used to assess the viability of HUVECs. First, HUVECs were cultured in 96-well plates (2×104 cells/mL, 100 μL) overnight. Following the instructions, 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent was added to the medium for 4 h. Then, the cell viability was assessed by measuring the optical density (OD) value at 450 nm.

sec.title: Apoptosis assay
sec.p: The Annexin V-FITC apoptosis assay kit (Cat. #C1062, Beyotime, Shanghai, China) was used to detect the apoptosis rate of HUVECs. First, cells were cultured in 12-well plates (1×105 cells/mL, 1 mL) overnight at 37°C in a 5% CO2 incubator. After the indicated treatments, 195 μL Annexin V-FITC binding buffer, 5 μL Annexin V-FITC and 10 μL propidium iodide (PI) was added to the medium for 20 min. Then, all collected cells were analyzed by a flow cytometer (Cytomics FC 500, Beckman Coulter Life Sciences, Brea, CA, USA).

sec.title: Cell migration assay
sec.p: The wound-healing assay was performed as previously described (Li et al., 2024). Microscopic images of the marked areas were captured immediately before (0 h) and 24 h after crebanine treatment. HUVECs in good growth condition were taken for starvation treatment for about 24 h. HUVECs (5×104 cells/mL) were resuspended with serum-free medium and later cultured into the upper chamber of 24-well transwell inserts (8.0-µm pore size; Corning, Shanghai, China), and 500 μL of complete culture medium was added to the lower chamber as a chemoattractant. After the indicated treatments, cells migrated through the porous membrane. Then, cells were gently removed from the upper chamber with a cotton swab, fixed in 4% methanol for 40 min and stained with 0.3% crystal violet for 15 min. Photographing and counting migrating cells under a fluorescence microscope (Nikon Eclipse TS2, Nikon, Tokyo, Japan).

sec.title: Tube formation assay
sec.p: HUVECs (1×106 cells/well) were seeded into 12-well plates pre-coated with Matrigel (Cat. #356230, Corning, NY, USA). Following treatment with LPS and crebanine, images of the tubular structures were captured using a microscope (Nikon Eclipse TS2, Nikon, Tokyo, Japan). The images were processed with ImageJ software (v1.8.0.112), and parameters such as tube length and branch points were quantified.

sec.title: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection and mitochondrial staining
sec.p: ROS generation was determined using a ROS Assay Kit (Cat. #S0033, Beyotime, Shanghai, China). The cells were maintained in the dark for 20 min in serum-free DMEM medium supplemented with 10 μM DCFH-DA. For mitochondrial fluorescence staining, DAPI and Mito-Tracker Green (Cat. #C1048, Beyotime, Shanghai, China) were used to label the nucleus and mitochondria, respectively. Finally, imaging was performed using a fluorescence microscope (488/525 nm excitation/emission) (Nikon Eclipse TS2, Nikon, Tokyo, Japan).

sec.title: Assay of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and malondialdehyde (MDA) contents
sec.p: The contents of SOD and MDA were measured using the commercial Detection Kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The absorbance at 450 nm was measured to detect the content of SOD, and the absorbance at 532 nm was measured to detect the content of MDA.

sec.title: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
sec.p: Cell supernatants were collected after the cells were treated accordingly. The levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) in the cell culture supernatants were detected according to the ELISA kit instructions (Invitrogen, CA, USA).

sec.title: qRT-PCR assay
sec.p: Total RNA of HUVECs was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). SYBR Green PCR kit (Accurate Biology, Hunan, China) was used for quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. The Primer sequences were as follows:
TNF, F: 5′-CCTCTCTCTAATCAGCCCTCTG-3′,
R: 5′-GAGGACCTGGGAGTAGATGAG-3′;
IL6, F: 5′-ATGATGGCTTATTACAGTGGCAA-3′,
R: 5′-GTCGGAGATTCGTAGCTGGA-3′;
IL1B, F: 5′-ACTCACCTCTTCAGAACGAATTG-3′,
R: 5′-CCATCTTTGGAAGGTTCAGGTTG-3′;
GAPDH, F: 5’-AGCCACATCGCTCAGACAC-3’,
R: 5’-GCCCAATACGACCAAATCC-3’.

sec.title: Western blotting analysis
sec.p: The protein was separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred to the PVDF membrane (Merck Millipore, Germany). The PVDF membrane were blocked at room temperature for 15 min using a a rapid sealing solution (EpiZyme, Shanghai, China) and then incubated with the following primary antibodies (rabbit anti-iNOS: 18985–1-AP; rabbit anti-p-p65 (Ser536): CST3033T; mouse anti-p65: CST6956T; rabbit anti-p-IκBα: CST2859T; rabbit anti-IκBα: CST4812T; rabbit anti-TNF-α: ab215188; rabbit anti-IL-6: ab233706; rabbit anti-IL-1β: ab234437; mouse anti-GAPDH: AF0006) overnight at 4°C. After washing with TBST 3 times (15 min each time), the PVDF membrane was incubated at room temperature for 1 h with a second antibody of the same species. Finally, the protein bands were visualized using ECL luminescence solution (Cat. #SQ201, EpiZyme, Shanghai, China).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The GraphPad Prism (v8.0.1, GraphPad Software Inc., La Jolla, CA, USA) was used to analyze data and create graph. Quantitative data were presented as the mean ± SEM. Differences between groups were analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by the Holm–Sidak multiple comparisons test (p<0.05 was statistically significant). All experiments were independently replicated at least three times.

sec.title: Crebanine ameliorates LPS-induced HUVECs injury
sec.p: The chemical structure of crebanine is shown in Fig. 1A. To determine the optimal LPS concentration for treating HUVECs, cells were exposed to 0-8 μg/mL LPS for 12 h. CCK-8 analysis revealed that 2 μg/mL LPS significantly inhibited cell viability, reducing the survival rate to approximately 50% (Fig. 1B). This inhibitory effect was also time-dependent (Fig. 1C). Consequently, based on these findings and supporting literature, an endothelial injury model was established by treating HUVECs with 2 μg/mL LPS for 12 h. Next, we assessed the effects of various concentrations of crebanine on HUVECs viability. As shown in Fig. 1D, neither DMSO nor crebanine at concentrations up to 40 μM significantly affected cell viability. Therefore, the subsequent experimental protocol involved stimulating HUVECs with 2 μg/mL LPS for 12 h, followed by treatment with 20 or 40 μM crebanine for 24 h (Fig. 1E). Consistent with the initial screening, 2 μg/mL LPS significantly suppressed HUVECs viability and promoted apoptosis compared to the control group. CCK-8 assay revealed that crebanine significantly improved the cell viability of LPS-treated HUVECs (Fig. 1F). Flow cytometry analysis showed that crebanine significantly protected HUVECs from LPS-induced apoptosis (Fig. 1G, 1H).

sec.title: Crebanine ameliorates LPS-impaired migration and tube formation in HUVECs
sec.p: Migration and tube formation capacities are essential for endothelial cells to maintain normal physiological functions. Chronic exposure of the vascular endothelium to an inflammatory environment compromises endothelial cell migration and tube formation, leading to reduced vasodilation, impaired neovascularization, and increased vascular permeability (Chang et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2025). Consistent with previous reports, our results demonstrated that LPS treatment significantly inhibited the migratory and tube-forming abilities of vascular endothelial cells. We employed two complementary assays to comprehensively evaluate the restorative effect of crebanine on LPS-impaired HUVECs migration, each focusing on a distinct aspect of cell motility. The wound healing assay, which measures the collective migration of a cell monolayer, revealed that crebanine significantly accelerated wound closure compared to the LPS-treated HUVECs (Fig. 2A, 2B). The Transwell migration assay, which assesses the chemotactic capacity of individual cells to traverse a membrane pore toward a chemoattractant gradient, demonstrated that crebanine markedly increased the number of migrated cells compared to the LPS group (Fig. 2C, 2D). Furthermore, we investigated the influence of crebanine on the tube-forming capacity of HUVECs under LPS challenge. The results indicated that LPS-stimulated HUVECs exhibited a remarkable reduction in tube-forming ability in vitro, characterized by decreased total tube length and number of branch points, compared with the control group (Fig. 2E). Crebanine treatment dose-dependently restored the tube-forming capacity of LPS-stimulated HUVECs (Fig. 2E, 2F). These findings suggest that crebanine significantly alleviates LPS-induced functional impairment in HUVECs and may possess preventive potential against the progression of endothelial dysfunction-related diseases.

sec.title: Crebanine improves oxidative stress and mitochondrial structural damage in HUVECs exposed to LPS
sec.p: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial structural damage are among the significant causes of dysfunction and decreased cell viability in LPS-treated HUVECs (Cui et al., 2018). We evaluated the effect of crebanine on LPS-induced oxidative stress in HUVECs. LPS stimulation significantly increased ROS production in HUVECs compared to the DMSO group, while ROS production was suppressed after crebanine treatment (Fig. 3A, 3B). Meanwhile, crebanine treatment under LPS stimulation elevated the levels of the antioxidant SOD and suppressed the production of MDA, a hallmark product of lipid peroxidation (Fig. 3C, 3D).

Furthermore, mitochondrial morphology was assessed using a mitochondria-specific green fluorescent probe (Mito-Tracker Green). Compared to the DMSO group, LPS-treated cells exhibited more swollen and fragmented mitochondria. In contrast, these structural alterations were significantly reversed in crebanine-treated cells, with mitochondria restoring their normal elongated morphology (Fig. 3E). These results demonstrate that crebanine can suppress oxidative stress and protect mitochondrial structure in LPS-exposed HUVECs.

sec.title: Crebanine inhibits the inflammatory response and NF-κB signaling pathway activation in HUVECs exposed to LPS
sec.p: The mRNA levels of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β were significantly elevated in HUVECs after LPS stimulation compared to controls. However, crebanine treatment significantly reduced LPS-induced TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β mRNA levels (Fig. 4A-4C). Additionally, ELISA results showed that crebanine treatment significantly decreased LPS-induced secretion of inflammatory factors (TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β) (Fig. 4D-4F).

The NF-κB signaling pathway plays an irreplaceable role in oxidative stress and inflammatory responses of endothelial cells (Chang et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023). Previous studies found that crebanine can regulate the NF-κB signaling pathway (Yang et al., 2023; Yodkeeree et al., 2014). Therefore, we speculated whether crebanine might inhibit LPS-induced oxidative stress and inflammation in endothelial cells by modulating the NF-κB signaling pathway. Western blotting results revealed that LPS activated the NF-κB signaling pathway in HUVECs, but crebanine attenuated this activation. Moreover, crebanine significantly decreased the protein levels of iNOS, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β (Fig. 5A-5C).

sec.title: Diprovocim counteracts the protection of crebanine on HUVECs exposed to LPS
sec.p: To further elucidate the mechanism of crebanine’s protection in LPS-stimulated HUVECs, we employed diprovocim, a known agonist of the NF-κB pathway. Diprovocim has been reported to promote NF-κB signaling by facilitating the degradation of IκBα or acting as a potent immunostimulant that engages Toll-like receptor pathways (Xu et al., 2025). CCK-8 results revealed that the cell viability of HUVECs in the crebanine+diprovocim group was significantly lower than that in the crebanine group (Fig. 6A). Importantly, diprovocim nullified the modulatory effects of crebanine on MDA and SOD in HUVECs exposed to LPS (Fig. 6B, 6C). Similarly, the inhibitory effect of crebanine on pro-inflammatory factors (TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β) in HUVECs exposed to LPS was significantly reduced by diprovocim (Fig. 6D-6F). Western blotting results revealed that diprovocim eliminated the modulatory effect of crebanine on NF-κB axis-related molecules p65 and IκB (Fig. 6G). Additionally, the inhibitory effect of crebanine on inflammatory factors (iNOS, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β) in HUVECs exposed to LPS was also reversed by diprovocim (Fig. 6H, 6I). These results further suggest that the mechanism by which crebanine ameliorates oxidative stress and inflammation in endothelial cells may be through the modulation of the NF-κB pathway.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Cardiovascular diseases pose a heavy socioeconomic burden, and the search for effective therapeutic agents has a great clinical importance (Schiattarella et al., 2021). In recent years, natural plant constituents with a variety of biological effects have attracted much attention. Crebanine is a monomer compound with potential pharmacological effects such as anti-inflammatory and analgesic, anti-arrhythmic, neuroprotective and anticancer (Dong et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2016; Yeh et al., 2024). In this study, we investigated for the first time the potential effects and possible mechanisms of crebanine on HUVECs exposed to LPS. The results suggest that crebanine improves cell viability and inhibits oxidative stress and inflammatory responses in LPS-stimulated HUVECs, at least in part by modulating the NF-κB signaling pathway (Fig. 7).

Endothelial cells are major members of the vasculature and have many important roles in maintaining systemic physiologic functions. Endothelial cells exposed to circulating blood are particularly susceptible to stimulation by pathogenic factors leading to cellular dysfunction, oxidative stress, and pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, which ultimately contribute to the development of vascular disease (Kremer et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2023). Oxidative stress is a state of cellular injury caused by overproduction of ROS or disruption of antioxidant defense mechanisms (Tang et al., 2025). ROS can directly damage endothelial cells leading to cellular dysfunction and apoptosis (Srivastava et al., 2025). Impairment of endothelial cell function leads to increased permeability of blood vessels, making it easier for harmful substances in the blood to diffuse into tissues (Ke et al., 2024). In addition, oxidative stress can promote atherosclerosis formation through oxidized low-density lipoprotein (Ox-LDL) (Wang et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023).

The inflammatory response is a natural defense mechanism made by the body in response to injury or infection (Shen et al., 2024). Activated endothelial cells can promote a localized inflammatory response by secreting inflammatory mediators such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β (D’Onofrio et al., 2023). Persistent chronic inflammation leads to remodeling of the vascular wall and increases the risk of vascular pathologies (Karabayas et al., 2024). Accumulating evidence suggests that oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis are not isolated events but are intricately linked in a self-amplifying vicious cycle, often referred to as the “oxidative stress–inflammation–apoptosis axis”, which plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis (Zhao et al., 2023). In this deleterious cascade, initial oxidative stress can activate pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, such as NF-κB, which in turn promotes the transcription of inflammatory cytokines (Xie et al., 2020). These cytokines can further recruit inflammatory cells and stimulate the production of more ROS, creating a positive feedback loop that exacerbates oxidative damage (Zhao et al., 2021). Ultimately, this sustained cellular insult leads to the activation of apoptotic pathways, resulting in cell death and tissue injury. Therapeutic strategies targeting oxidative stress and inflammation show important potential in the prevention and treatment of vascular disease.

NF-κB is a family of transcription factors that play key roles in cellular responses to stress and immune reactions (Kannan et al., 2025). Especially in vascular endothelial cells, NF-κB is a central regulator of oxidative stress and inflammatory responses (Cho et al., 2023). Stimulation of cells causes activation of IκB kinase (IKK), which phosphorylates the IκB protein, leading to its degradation and the release of NF-κB complexed with IκB (Liu et al., 2025). Free-form NF-κB (p65) translocates to the nucleus and initiates the expression of a number of genes related to oxidative stress and inflammation (Chu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024). Crebanine, an alkaloid of the aporphine class, is widely present in a variety of herbs in nature. In the present study, we found that crebanine may ameliorate endothelial cell oxidative stress and inflammation by inhibiting the NF-κB signaling axis. Additionally, the protective effects of crebanine were partially reversed by diprovocim. However, since diprovocim is not specific to NF-κB and may affect multiple downstream targets, the results of this study still cannot determine whether NF-κB is the sole mediator. Another limitation of this study is the lack of in vivo validation. Future studies should include animal models to verify these results in a whole-organism context.

In conclusion, the results of the present study suggest that crebanine might attenuate oxidative stress and inflammatory responses in HUVECs exposed to LPS conditions by inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway, ultimately improving endothelial cell function. These exciting findings suggest that crebanine may have the potential to improve vascular endothelial cell function and treat vascular diseases. In addition, crebanine’s potential anti-inflammatory activity in other diseases is an interesting matter to be further explored.
